This vignette is a guided tour of the functions of `biblionetwork`, using the
data included in the package (see @sec-data). Every function turns a **table of
links between two kinds of items** (for instance documents and the references
they cite) into the **edges of a network** whose nodes are one of the two
kinds, with a weight for each edge. The functions differ by the kind of nodes
and by the way the weight is computed.

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
library(biblionetwork)
library(data.table)
```

| You want to link... | Because they... | Function |
|---|---|---|
| citing documents | share references [@kessler1963] | `biblio_coupling()` (see @sec-coupling) |
| cited references | are cited together [@small1973] | `biblio_cocitation()` (see @sec-cocitation) |
| authors, journals, institutions | cite the same references (or are cited together) through their documents [@zhao2008b] | `entity_network()` (see @sec-entity) |
| authors, institutions, countries | co-sign documents | `coauth_network()` (see @sec-coauthorship) |

: Which function for which network? {#tbl-functions}

# The data included in the package {#sec-data}

The package contains bibliometric data built by @goutsmedt2021a: the academic
articles and books, published between 1975 and 2013, that tried to explain the
US stagflation of the 1970s, and the references they cite.

* `Ref_stagflation` is a table of **direct citations**: one row per link
  between a citing document (`Citing_ItemID_Ref`) and a cited document
  (`ItemID_Ref`). It is the typical input of the coupling and co-citation
  functions.
* `Nodes_stagflation` describes the stagflation documents, and the references
  cited by at least two of them (one row per document, with the first author
  only).
* `Authors_stagflation` lists the stagflation documents with *all* their
  authors (one row per author and document). It is the input of the
  co-authorship function.

```{r}
#| label: data
Ref_stagflation[1:5, 1:2]
```

Every function of the package needs only **two columns of identifiers**,
that you name in the arguments `source` and `ref`. The names of the columns in
your own data do not matter, and the table you give is never modified.

# Bibliographic coupling: `biblio_coupling()` {#sec-coupling}

Two documents are *bibliographically coupled* when they cite the same
references [@kessler1963]: the more their bibliographies overlap, the more
likely they are to address related questions. `biblio_coupling()` takes a
table of direct citations and returns the list of the pairs of documents that
share at least one reference, with a weight for each pair.

```{r}
#| label: coupling-default
edges <- biblio_coupling(Ref_stagflation,
                         source = "Citing_ItemID_Ref",
                         ref = "ItemID_Ref",
                         normalized_weight_only = FALSE)
edges
```

The output is an **edge list**:

* `from` and `to` are the identifiers of the two documents (as characters, which
  is what graph packages such as `tidygraph` expect; set
  `output_in_character = FALSE` to skip them);
* `weight` is the weight of the tie;
* `nb_shared_references` is the number of references the two documents share.
  It is displayed only if `normalized_weight_only = FALSE`;
* `Source` and `Target` keep the original identifiers (with their original
  type). Each pair appears once, with `Source < Target`: the network is
  undirected.

## The default weight: the coupling angle

By default, the weight is the **coupling angle** (or cosine) of @sen1983, the
standard way of normalising coupling. It divides the number of references two
documents share by the geometric mean of the lengths of their bibliographies:

$$
w_{AB} = \frac{|R(A) \cap R(B)|}{\sqrt{L(A) \, L(B)}}
$$

where $R(A)$ is the set of references of document $A$, $|R(A) \cap R(B)|$ the
number of references shared by $A$ and $B$, and $L(A) = |R(A)|$ the length of the
bibliography of $A$. Without the denominator, a literature review with 200
references would be linked to almost everybody, simply because it cites a lot.
The weight lies between 0 (nothing in common) and 1 (identical
bibliographies). The same measure is available under its own name,
`coupling_angle()`, which is what `biblio_coupling()` calls when you do not
choose another `method`.

::: {.callout-note}
## What counts as the length of a bibliography?
$L(A)$ counts *all* the references of $A$ present in your table, including
those that no other document cites. They cannot create a tie, but they make the
bibliography longer, and so they lower the weights of $A$. If you want to ignore
them, remove them from the table before calling the function.
:::

## Choosing the minimal number of shared references

In a large corpus, sharing a single reference is weak evidence that two
documents are related, and keeping all such pairs produces very dense networks.
`weight_threshold` sets the minimal number of shared references for a pair to be
kept. It applies to the *number of shared references*, not to the normalised
weight.

```{r}
#| label: coupling-threshold
biblio_coupling(Ref_stagflation,
                source = "Citing_ItemID_Ref",
                ref = "ItemID_Ref",
                weight_threshold = 3)
```

Raising the threshold is also the simplest way to keep a network tractable.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Very popular references and memory
The functions first list the pairs of documents that cite a same reference. A
reference cited by $n$ documents creates $n(n-1)/2$ pairs: a classic cited by
50,000 documents creates more than a billion of them. The package uses sparse
matrices to keep this under control, but very popular references can still
exhaust the memory of your computer on a large corpus. Split the corpus (by
time window, for instance) or remove the most cited references before building
the network.
:::

## Other weights: the `method` argument {#sec-methods}

The coupling angle gives the same importance to every shared reference. But two
documents that both cite a classic cited by half of the corpus are not as
clearly related as two documents that both cite an obscure article. Several
measures take this into account, in the spirit of the
[tf-idf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tf%E2%80%93idf) weighting of
information retrieval [@sparckjones1972]. They are all available through the
`method` argument of `biblio_coupling()`, and each has its own function:

| `method` | Function | Intuition |
|---|---|---|
| `"angle"` (default) | `coupling_angle()` | Shared references relative to the length of the two bibliographies (a cosine) [@sen1983]. |
| `"jaccard"` | `coupling_jaccard()` | Of everything the two documents cite, the share they both cite [@sen1983]. |
| `"strength"` | `coupling_strength()` | A shared *rare* reference counts more than a shared classic [@vladutz1984; @shen2019]. |
| `"similarity"` | `coupling_similarity()` | The same idea, as a cosine bounded by 1 [@shen2019]. |
| `"vladutz"` | `coupling_vladutz()` | A shared reference counts $1/f_j$: a very steep discount of popular references [@vladutz1984]. |

: The weights of document coupling {#tbl-methods}

In the formulas below, $N$ is the number of citing documents in the table and
$f_j$ the number of documents that cite the reference $j$ (its *frequency*): the
weight $\log(N/f_j)$ of a reference is the inverse document frequency (idf), high for
rare references and close to zero for references cited by almost everybody.

**Coupling strength** [@shen2019] sums the idf of the shared references, and
divides by the lengths of the two bibliographies:

$$
w_{AB} = \frac{1}{L(A) \, L(B)} \sum_{j \in R(A) \cap R(B)} \log\left(\frac{N}{f_j}\right)
$$

Use it when a few references are cited by most documents of your corpus (the
classics of the field): sharing them says little about the proximity of two
documents. The price is a measure that depends on the whole corpus, and whose
scale (it is not bounded by 1) is not comparable across corpora.

```{r}
#| label: coupling-strength
biblio_coupling(Ref_stagflation,
                source = "Citing_ItemID_Ref",
                ref = "ItemID_Ref",
                method = "strength",
                weight_threshold = 3)
```

**Coupling similarity** [@shen2019, Eq. 8] is the idf-weighted cosine. Each
document is described by the "informational size" of its bibliography,
$S(A) = \sum_{j \in R(A)} \log(N/f_j)$, and

$$
w_{AB} = \frac{\sum_{j \in R(A) \cap R(B)} \log(N/f_j)}{\sqrt{S(A) \, S(B)}}
$$

It generalises the coupling angle (if all the references had the same idf, we
would get the angle back) and is bounded by 1.

```{r}
#| label: coupling-similarity
coupling_similarity(Ref_stagflation,
                    source = "Citing_ItemID_Ref",
                    ref = "ItemID_Ref",
                    weight_threshold = 3)
```

The two other measures are mostly useful for comparison. `coupling_jaccard()`
divides the number of shared references by the size of the *union* of the two
bibliographies, and penalises more strongly pairs of bibliographies of very
different lengths. `coupling_vladutz()` implements the first formula that
discounted popular references [@vladutz1984], which @shen2019 later corrected
with the idf.

## Comparing the measures on your corpus

The measures do not have the same scale, so their weights cannot be compared
directly, but their distributions and rankings can. `compute_couplings()`
computes several measures at once (listing the pairs of documents only once),
and `summarise_weights()`, `correlate_weights()`, `overlap_top_weights()`,
`merge_weights()` and `plot_weights()` compare them.

```{r}
#| label: compare
measures <- compute_couplings(Ref_stagflation,
                              source = "Citing_ItemID_Ref",
                              ref = "ItemID_Ref",
                              weight_threshold = 2)
# Rank correlation between the measures (1 = the same ranking of the pairs)
round(correlate_weights(measures), 2)
```

Whether the choice of the measure matters on your corpus, which pairs of
documents the measures disagree on, and how the communities change is the
subject of [the vignette on comparing measures](comparing_measures.html).

# Co-citation: `biblio_cocitation()` {#sec-cocitation}

Coupling links the documents that *cite*; co-citation links the documents that
are *cited*: two references are co-cited when a same document cites both
[@small1973]. It is the mirror image of coupling, and it is obtained by
swapping the roles of the two columns. `biblio_cocitation()` does the swap for
you: the citing documents stay in `source` and the references in `ref`, and the
nodes of the network are the references.

```{r}
#| label: cocitation
biblio_cocitation(Ref_stagflation,
                  source = "Citing_ItemID_Ref",
                  ref = "ItemID_Ref",
                  weight_threshold = 2)
```

You get the same result by hand with `biblio_coupling()`, by inverting the two
columns:

```{r}
#| label: cocitation-by-hand
by_hand <- biblio_coupling(Ref_stagflation,
                           source = "ItemID_Ref",
                           ref = "Citing_ItemID_Ref",
                           weight_threshold = 2)
all.equal(by_hand, biblio_cocitation(Ref_stagflation,
                                     source = "Citing_ItemID_Ref",
                                     ref = "ItemID_Ref",
                                     weight_threshold = 2))
```

`biblio_cocitation()` also has a `method` argument, with the same measures as
coupling. There is a difference of interpretation, though: coupling ties are
fixed once the documents are published (they depend only on their own
bibliographies), whereas co-citation ties change as new documents cite the
references. Coupling is therefore better suited to comparing successive time
windows, and co-citation to describing how a literature is perceived at a given
moment.

# Aggregating at the level of entities: `entity_network()` {#sec-entity}

You may want to link authors, institutions or journals rather than documents.
This is not a different kind of network, nor a different measure: it is the
*same* coupling (or co-citation), computed for entities that aggregate
documents. An entity publishes several documents and can cite the same
reference several times. `entity_network()` takes this into account: for each
reference shared by two entities, it counts the **minimum** number of times the
two entities cite it [@zhao2008b]. If one author cites a reference in two of
their articles and another in three, the reference counts for two.

The consequence is that a reference that two entities cite repeatedly
contributes more to the tie than a reference each of them cites once. With the
coupling strength, the weight is

$$
w_{AB} = \frac{1}{L(A) \, L(B)} \sum_{j} \min(C_{Aj}, C_{Bj}) \, \log\left(\frac{N}{f_j}\right)
$$

where $C_{Aj}$ and $C_{Bj}$ are the numbers of times $A$ and $B$ cite the
reference $j$, $L(A)$ is the total number of citations made by $A$, $N$ the number of citing
documents and $f_j$ the number of documents citing $j$. The `method` argument
accepts the same methods as `biblio_coupling()` (`"angle"`, `"strength"`,
`"similarity"`, `"jaccard"` and `"vladutz"`), each adapted with the minimum
rule (see `?entity_network` for the formulas), and the `network` argument
chooses between `"coupling"` (entities that cite the same references) and
`"cocitation"` (entities whose references are cited together, as in author
co-citation analysis).

The input needs one row per citation *and* per entity: we merge the table of
direct citations with the table of authors. A document with several authors
appears several times, hence `allow.cartesian = TRUE`.

```{r}
#| label: entity-network
entity_citations <- merge(Ref_stagflation,
                          Authors_stagflation,
                          by.x = "Citing_ItemID_Ref",
                          by.y = "ItemID_Ref",
                          allow.cartesian = TRUE)

entity_network(entity_citations,
               source = "Citing_ItemID_Ref",
               ref = "ItemID_Ref",
               entity = "Author.y",
               method = "angle")
```

For a co-citation network of entities, the `entity` column must describe the
*cited* reference (the author or the journal of the cited document) rather than
the citing one. Here, the journals of the cited documents:

```{r}
#| label: entity-cocitation
entity_network(Ref_stagflation,
                    source = "Citing_ItemID_Ref",
                    ref = "ItemID_Ref",
                    entity = "Journal",
                    network = "cocitation",
                    weight_threshold = 3)
```

# Co-authorship: `coauth_network()` {#sec-coauthorship}

Co-authorship links the authors (or institutions, or countries) who sign
documents together. You could build it with `biblio_coupling()`, authors being
the `source` and documents the `ref`, but coupling is not designed for it: what
matters here is how to **count a collaboration**. `coauth_network()` offers
three ways, and an optional normalisation by the productivity of the authors.

To see what they do, take a toy example: three authors, $a$, $b$ and $c$, sign
document 1; $a$ and $b$ sign document 2.

```{r}
#| label: coauth-toy
toy <- data.frame(author = c("a", "b", "c", "a", "b"),
                  paper  = c(1, 1, 1, 2, 2))
```

**Full counting** (`"full_counting"`) gives one point to each pair of authors for
each document they co-sign. The weight is the number of co-signed documents.
Here $a$–$b$ gets 2 points, and $a$–$c$ and $b$–$c$ one point each. The problem is
that big collaborations weigh more: a document with ten authors creates 45
pairs, so it adds 45 points to the network, whereas a document with two
authors adds one.

```{r}
#| label: coauth-full
coauth_network(toy, authors = "author", articles = "paper", method = "full_counting")
```

**Fractional counting** (`"fractional_counting"`) shares the value of a document
among the co-authors, so that a large collaboration does not dominate
[@perianes-rodriguez2016b]. A document with $n$ authors gives $1/(n-1)$ to each
pair of its authors, so that the weights of all the ties of an author in this
document sum to one: each author "spends" one unit of collaboration per
document, split among the co-authors. In the toy example, document 1 has three
authors, so each of its three pairs receives $1/2$; document 2 has two authors,
so $a$–$b$ receives $1$. The weight of $a$–$b$ is $1/2 + 1 = 1.5$, and that of
$a$–$c$ and $b$–$c$ is $1/2$: the pair that collaborated in a small team is
worth more than a pair in a large team. @perianes-rodriguez2016b compare full
and fractional counting on bibliometric networks, and show that the choice
changes the picture.

```{r}
#| label: coauth-fractional
coauth_network(toy, authors = "author", articles = "paper", method = "fractional_counting")
```

**Refined fractional counting** (`"fractional_counting_refined"`), inspired by
@leydesdorff2017, goes one step further: each *document*, rather than each
author, has a total weight of one in the network. A document with $n$ authors
creates $n(n-1)/2$ pairs, so each pair gets $2/(n(n-1))$. Document 1 gives
$1/3$ to each of its three pairs ($3 \times 1/3 = 1$) and document 2 gives $1$
to $a$–$b$. The weight of $a$–$b$ is $1/3 + 1 \approx 1.33$. The sum of all the
weights of the network is then the number of co-authored documents.

```{r}
#| label: coauth-refined
coauth_network(toy, authors = "author", articles = "paper", method = "fractional_counting_refined")
```

In all cases, documents with a single author are ignored, since they create no
tie.

**Normalising by productivity.** Prolific authors have many collaborations
simply because they publish a lot. With `cosine_normalized = TRUE`, the weight
is divided by $\sqrt{P_i P_j}$, where $P_i$ is the number of co-authored
documents of author $i$ (Salton's cosine, as for the coupling angle). The weight
then measures whether two authors collaborate a lot *relative to* how much each
of them collaborates in general. In the toy example, $P_a = P_b = 2$ and
$P_c = 1$: with full counting, $a$–$b$ gets $2/\sqrt{2 \times 2} = 1$ and $a$–$c$
gets $1/\sqrt{2 \times 1} \approx 0.71$.

```{r}
#| label: coauth-cosine
coauth_network(toy, authors = "author", articles = "paper",
               method = "full_counting", cosine_normalized = TRUE)
```

On the stagflation authors, with fractional counting and the cosine
normalisation:

```{r}
#| label: coauth-stagflation
coauth_network(Authors_stagflation,
               authors = "Author",
               articles = "ItemID_Ref",
               method = "fractional_counting",
               cosine_normalized = TRUE)
```

Note that, for historical reasons, `coauth_network()` orients its edges with
`Source > Target`, the opposite of the other functions.

# Filtering the edges: thresholds and backbones {#sec-backbone}

A bibliometric network built from a large corpus is often too dense to be read
or clustered: almost every pair of documents shares at least one reference.
There are two ways of simplifying it.

* **A threshold**, as seen above: `weight_threshold` keeps the pairs sharing at
  least $k$ references. It is simple and fast, but arbitrary, and it is
  *global*: the same threshold applies to a document with a hundred references
  and to a document with five.
* **A backbone**: keep only the ties that are statistically unlikely under a
  null model, that is, the ties that are stronger than what the position of
  the nodes in the network would produce by chance. This is the aim of the
  [`backbone`](https://github.com/zpneal/backbone) package [@neal2026], which
  is complementary to `biblionetwork`: `biblionetwork` computes the edges and their weights,
  `backbone` decides which ones are worth keeping.

`backbone` offers two families of methods, and they do not start from the same
object.

**Filters of weighted networks** (`backbone_from_weighted()`, with the disparity
filter of @serrano2009 for instance) start from a *weighted one-mode network*.
They can be run directly on the edges produced by `biblionetwork`: convert the
edge list into a graph and give it to `backbone`. Since these filters assume that the weights are
strengths of ties, it is more natural to feed them with the *number of shared
references* (`normalized_weight_only = FALSE`) than with a cosine.

```{r}
#| label: backbone-weighted
#| eval: !expr requireNamespace("backbone", quietly = TRUE) && requireNamespace("igraph", quietly = TRUE)
edges <- biblio_coupling(Ref_stagflation,
                         source = "Citing_ItemID_Ref",
                         ref = "ItemID_Ref",
                         normalized_weight_only = FALSE,
                         weight_threshold = 2)

# The weighted graph; the number of shared references is the weight
graph <- igraph::graph_from_data_frame(
  edges[, .(from, to, weight = nb_shared_references)],
  directed = FALSE
)

# The disparity filter: keep an edge if its weight is significantly high
# compared to the other edges of (at least one of) its two nodes
backbone <- backbone::backbone_from_weighted(graph, model = "disparity", alpha = 0.05)
c(edges_before = igraph::ecount(graph), edges_after = igraph::ecount(backbone))
```

**Filters of bipartite projections** (`backbone_from_projection()`, with
models such as `"sdsm"`, the stochastic degree sequence model) do not start from
the edges but from the *original two-mode table*: they compare the number of
references that two documents share with the number expected if documents cited
references at random, given how many references each document cites and how
many documents cite each reference. The input is the table of citations as an
incidence matrix (documents in rows, references in columns), which is the same
table as the one you give to `biblionetwork`.

```{r}
#| label: backbone-projection
#| eval: !expr requireNamespace("backbone", quietly = TRUE) && requireNamespace("igraph", quietly = TRUE)
# Incidence matrix of the citations: 1 if the document (row) cites the reference (column)
incidence <- unclass(table(Ref_stagflation$Citing_ItemID_Ref, Ref_stagflation$ItemID_Ref))
incidence[incidence > 1] <- 1

# Statistically significant coupling ties (the filter is applied to the rows)
backbone_sdsm <- backbone::backbone_from_projection(incidence, model = "sdsm", alpha = 0.05)
sum(backbone_sdsm) / 2   # number of ties kept (the matrix is symmetric)
```

Two practical remarks.

* The statistical models test the *count* of shared references, not a
  normalised weight. Run them on the full table, **without** a
  `weight_threshold`: a pair removed by the threshold cannot be tested. The
  backbone then replaces the threshold. You can use `biblionetwork` afterwards,
  on the pairs kept, if you want the normalised weights of the surviving ties
  (merge the two edge lists by pair of documents).
* These tests are computationally heavier than the edge computation of
  `biblionetwork`, and the null models are not designed for the huge corpora
  that `biblionetwork` handles: on a large corpus, split it by time window, or
  start from the filters of weighted networks.

`networkflow` integrates both steps: its function `build_dynamic_networks()`
can compute the coupling edges and apply a statistical backbone for each time
window (see the [`networkflow`](https://agoutsmedt.github.io/networkflow/)
documentation).

# Beyond bibliometrics {#sec-beyond}

Nothing in the functions of `biblionetwork` is specific to bibliography. They
take a table with two columns, "a *source* that is linked to a *ref*", and
build the network of the sources that share refs (coupling) or of the refs
that share sources (co-citation). The words "document" and "reference" are only
the vocabulary of the field in which the package was written. Whenever you have
a two-mode relation, the same questions can be asked:

| Source ("citing") | Ref ("cited") | Coupling links sources that... | Co-citation links refs that... |
|---|---|---|---|
| article | reference | cite the same references | are cited by the same articles |
| social media account | account followed | follow the same accounts (an audience in common) | are followed by the same accounts |
| social media account | post reposted | repost the same posts | are reposted by the same accounts |
| post | hashtag, link, mention | use the same hashtags, links or mentions | are used in the same posts |
| document | word | use the same words | appear in the same documents |

: A two-mode table, many networks {#tbl-beyond}

## Networks of accounts on a social media platform

Take a table of the accounts of a social media platform and the accounts
they follow. Two accounts that follow many of the same accounts probably listen
to the same voices: this is the bibliographic coupling of the "follows" (the
account is the "document", the accounts it follows are its "bibliography"). In
the same way, two accounts that repost the same posts are close in what they
amplify. The following table is invented, for the sake of the example.

```{r}
#| label: social-toy
follows <- data.table(
  account = c("ann", "ann", "ann", "ben", "ben", "ben", "cleo", "cleo", "dan", "dan", "eve", "eve", "eve"),
  follows = c("news_desk", "dev_tools", "open_web", "news_desk", "dev_tools", "open_web",
              "news_desk", "celebrity", "celebrity", "news_desk", "celebrity", "dev_tools", "open_web")
)

# Accounts close because they follow the same accounts
biblio_coupling(follows, source = "account", ref = "follows", normalized_weight_only = FALSE)
```

Here `news_desk` and `celebrity` are followed by almost everybody: following
them says little. The idf-based methods, designed for the "classics" of
a bibliography, are exactly what is needed to discount the accounts followed by
a large audience:

```{r}
#| label: social-strength
biblio_coupling(follows, source = "account", ref = "follows", method = "strength")
```

This is how coupling is used on social media data: popular targets (an account
followed by millions) are the equivalent of the classics of a field, and the
warning on memory of @sec-coupling matters even more, as such targets are
much more frequent than in a bibliography. Reposts work the same way, with
`source` the account and `ref` the reposted post. And co-citation answers the
mirror question: *which posts are reposted by the same accounts?*

```{r}
#| label: social-cocitation
reposts <- data.table(
  account = c("ann", "ann", "ben", "ben", "cleo", "cleo", "dan"),
  post    = c("p1", "p2", "p1", "p2", "p2", "p3", "p3")
)
biblio_cocitation(reposts, source = "account", ref = "post")
```

Because a network of this kind is often dense (and the measures do not tell
which ties are "surprising"), the backbone of @sec-backbone is particularly
useful there.

## Networks of words

A text is a "document" that "cites" words. The coupling of texts links the texts
that use the same words; the co-citation of words links the words that appear
together. We illustrate it with the titles of the stagflation documents.

```{r}
#| label: words-prepare
titles <- Nodes_stagflation[!is.na(Title), .(ItemID_Ref, Title)]

# One row per title and distinct word. Short words and a few stop words are dropped:
# like popular references, very frequent words create a huge number of pairs and carry little meaning.
stop_words <- c("the", "and", "for", "with", "from", "that", "this", "its", "are", "was",
                "into", "their", "between", "some", "what", "how", "when", "than", "have", "new")
words <- titles[, .(word = unique(tolower(unlist(strsplit(Title, "[^A-Za-z]+"))))), by = ItemID_Ref]
words <- words[nchar(word) > 3 & !word %in% stop_words]
words[1:5]
```

Titles are coupled when they share words. The coupling strength gives more
weight to rare words than to words such as "inflation" or "policy", present in
many titles:

```{r}
#| label: words-coupling
title_edges <- biblio_coupling(words, source = "ItemID_Ref", ref = "word",
                               method = "strength", normalized_weight_only = FALSE,
                               weight_threshold = 2)
title_edges[order(-weight)][1:5]
```

Words are linked when they appear in the same titles (this is the co-citation
of words). The words that always appear together are the fixed expressions of
the corpus:

```{r}
#| label: words-cooccurrence
word_edges <- biblio_cocitation(words, source = "ItemID_Ref", ref = "word",
                                weight_threshold = 2, normalized_weight_only = FALSE)
word_edges[order(-nb_shared_citations)][1:8, .(from, to, weight, nb_shared_citations)]
```

The same logic applies to any "bag of ..." representation (n-grams, keywords,
hashtags, named entities, topics of a topic model...). For the words in the
titles of references, `coupling_descriptive()` implements a more elaborate
approach [@liu2017], which couples documents that cite *different but related*
references.

## What to check before using it outside bibliometrics

* **Orientation.** `source` is the node of the network produced by `biblio_coupling()`;
  `ref` is what the nodes share. If the network you obtain has the wrong nodes, you
  probably swapped the columns (the function warns you when no pair is found).
* **Popular targets.** A target shared by very many sources (a celebrity, a
  stop word) creates a quadratic number of pairs and carries little
  information. Remove it, or use a method that discounts it, or work by time window.
* **The meaning of "length".** The normalisation by the length of the
  bibliography assumes that having many refs is a form of dilution. For an account
  following 10,000 accounts, this is reasonable; for a text, the length of the
  document in words may be a different matter.
* **Time.** Coupling ties are fixed when the source is created. For social media data,
  the "follows" are not dated in the same way as references: think about the
  moment at which the table is observed.

# A last word on choosing {#sec-choose}

| Question | Nodes | Function |
|---|---|---|
| Which documents rely on the same literature? Which research fronts? [@kessler1963; @boyack2010] | citing documents | `biblio_coupling()` |
| Same, but not driven by the classics of the corpus [@shen2019] | citing documents | `biblio_coupling(method = "strength")` or `"similarity"` |
| Does the choice of the measure matter on my corpus? | citing documents | `compute_couplings()`, then `correlate_weights()`, `plot_weights()` |
| Which authors, journals or institutions rely on the same literature (or are cited together)? [@zhao2008b] | entities | `entity_network()` |
| Which cited texts are perceived as belonging together? [@small1973] | cited references | `biblio_cocitation()` |
| Who collaborates with whom? [@perianes-rodriguez2016b; @leydesdorff2017] | authors, institutions, countries | `coauth_network()` |
| Which of these ties are not due to chance? [@neal2026] | any | the `backbone` package |

: Which measure for which research question? {#tbl-questions}

All the functions return undirected edges (one row per pair), never modify the table you give them,
and return an empty table, with a warning that says why, when no pair of nodes is linked.
